content.text:
Does this text message actually offer that CO will call THEM — Cue proposing to place an outbound call to the person, not just telling them how they can call Cue themselves — in any wording, even indirectly (e.g. "I'm here if you want to talk this through")? Not just related to talking or listening in general — specifically Cue offering to call them.

Message: "Say it's a Noise dinner next month. Two guests, call them Dana and Priya, both RSVP yes. Before the event I ask each of them which of their asks I can mention to a good match, and whether I can use their name in the brief. Dana says yes to both, Priya says yes to the ask but no to her name. The morning of, Dana texts me "here" and Priya shares her location for the event. That's when I start telling each of them, one on one, who's worth meeting and why, based on what they told me and what the other guests told me, never crossing wires.

Say I tell Dana that Priya's working on something close to what she's looking for. I mention Priya's ask, since she said yes to that, but I use "a guest" not her name, since she said no there. If Dana wants to meet her, that's a yes from Dana.

I'd then check with Priya the same way, with Dana's ask and name, since Dana said yes to both. If Priya also says yes, I send one email to both of them together, and they take it from there, it's not me setting up a time.

After the dinner, I follow up with each of them and ask how the meeting went. That answer is what shapes who I'd point either of them to next time."

Return ONLY "yes" or "no".
